title: Purpose and result

objectives.can: Recognise purpose and result expressed by לְ with the infinitive, לְמַעַן, בַּעֲבוּר, פֶּן, and by a volitive form after another.

explanation.summary: Hebrew can say 'in order to', 'so that', 'lest' and 'so that not' in several ways: an infinitive with לְ, the particles לְמַעַן and בַּעֲבוּר, the particle פֶּן, and a wish or command followed by another. Purpose, the end someone aims at, and result, the end that follows, are often hard to tell apart, and the lesson shows how to weigh them.

sections.heading: Purpose and result are neighbours
body: A purpose clause says what someone intends: 'he went up in order to pray'. A result clause says what actually followed: 'he prayed so that the whole house heard'. In English the two are different constructions. In Hebrew the same forms often serve for both, and grammarians say that the sense is sometimes a matter of the reader's judgement.

A useful test is to ask whether anyone intends the end. If the subject of the main clause aims at it, it is purpose. If the end only follows from what was done, it is result. Where the speaker is God or a person whose mind is not shown, the test does not settle the matter. The lesson ends with a verse on which readers divide.

sections.heading: לְ with the infinitive construct
body: The commonest way to give a purpose is the infinitive construct with the prefix לְ, placed after the main verb: 'the LORD came down to see the city'; 'I have come down to deliver them'. It is often found after verbs of going, sending, coming and putting. The subject of the infinitive is usually the subject of the main verb; a suffix on the infinitive can give the object, as in לְהַצִּילוֹ, 'to deliver him'.

The same construction can also give a result or a bare completion of the verb, and it can be a noun-like complement ('the time to build'). The context tells you which. A purpose infinitive follows a verb that can sensibly have an aim.

To say 'so as not to', Hebrew uses לְבִלְתִּי with an infinitive: the sign set on Cain was 'so that no one would strike him'. The negative לְבִלְתִּי is one word, and it is not the same as the simple negative לֹא.

sections.heading: לְמַעַן and בַּעֲבוּר
body: לְמַעַן and בַּעֲבוּר are the particles most often rendered 'in order that'. Each stands before a yiqtol (or a jussive) to say what the action is for: לְמַעַן תִּחְיוּ, 'so that you may live'. Each may also stand before an infinitive: לְמַעַן חַלֵּל, 'in order to profane' or 'so that … profane'.

Both words also have other uses. בַּעֲבוּר can be a preposition, 'for the sake of' (בַעֲבוּרֵךְ, 'for your sake'), and it can mean 'because of' as well as 'in order to'. The order of the words and the verb after them decide. In Deuteronomy the particle לְמַעַן is very frequent, and often several such clauses follow one commandment, each naming a further aim.

sections.heading: פֶּן: lest
body: פֶּן introduces a clause that names something feared or to be avoided, and the main clause says what to do about it. 'Go down, charge the people, lest they break through' means: do this in order that they should not. The verb after פֶּן is generally a yiqtol.
The danger often grows into a series. After פֶּן a weqatal can carry on the description of what is feared, as in Pharaoh's speech in Exodus 1:10, where one dreaded event leads to the next.
Notice that פֶּן is the speaker's fear, not a statement of fact. What is feared may or may not come about.

sections.heading: A wish or command followed by another
body: Hebrew often puts a purpose or consequence into a second volitive form, with no word for 'so that' at all. An imperative may be followed by וְ and a cohortative or jussive: 'go down … and let us live'. The second form states the end that the first is meant to reach. Grammarians call this a final or consequential sequence of volitives, and it is common in speech.

The same logic holds in the ordinary narrative of intentions. A weqatal after a command or a yiqtol can give the result that follows when the command is carried out. In this lesson the pattern is shown on a real verse, and the later lessons on the verbal system return to it.

head: Means
What it tends to signal
Verb form
rows: purpose, often after a verb of motion
something feared or to be avoided: 'lest'
the end the command aims at: 'so that'

misunderstandings: לְ with an infinitive does not always give a purpose. It can supply a complement, and a result or a bare completion. Look at the main verb to see whether it has an aim.
פֶּן is not 'if not'. It names what the speaker fears, and the main clause says what to do to avoid it.
לְמַעַן does not always mean the speaker intended the end. Some grammarians read certain uses as result, and the question can be open.
A cohortative after an imperative is not a second, separate command. It usually states the end the first one aims at.

deeper.heading: Purpose or result in Amos 2:7?
body: Amos 2:7 charges that a man and his father go to the same girl לְמַעַן חַלֵּל אֶת שֵׁם קָדְשִׁי. If לְמַעַן is read as purpose, the clause says the men do it in order to profane the holy name, which the Hebrew would make a deliberate aim. If it is read as result, the clause says that the effect of their conduct is that the name is profaned, without ascribing that aim to them. Both readings are grammatically possible, since לְמַעַן is found with both senses, and translations divide.

The first reading follows the commonest use of the particle. The second is preferred by readers who doubt that the prophet charges the men with intending the profanation. The grammar cannot settle between them; the context and the reader's view of the prophet's rhetoric will have to.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Purpose with לְ and the infinitive construct. The man is put in the garden לְעָבְדָהּ וּלְשָׁמְרָהּ, 'to work it and to keep it'. The suffix on each infinitive is the object, 'it' (the garden), and the subject is the man. Two infinitives joined by וְ give two aims.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Say, I pray thee, thou art my sister; that it may be well with me for thy sake, and that my soul may live because of thee.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: An imperative, אִמְרִי, 'say', is followed by לְמַעַן and a yiqtol, יִיטַב, 'that it may go well with me'. The weqatal וְחָיְתָה adds a second aim. Notice the noun בַעֲבוּרֵךְ, 'for your sake', where בַּעֲבוּר is a preposition and has a suffix; the same word as a particle introduces a clause in other verses.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And they said: 'Come, let us build us a city, and a tower, with its top in heaven, and let us make us a name; lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two cohortatives, נִבְנֶה and נַעֲשֶׂה, follow הָבָה, 'come': 'let us build … and let us make for ourselves a name'. Then פֶּן־ names the fear that drives the plan: lest we be scattered, with the yiqtol נָפוּץ. The fear explains the purpose of the building.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And he said: 'Behold, I have heard that there is corn in Egypt. Get you down thither, and buy for us from thence; that we may live, and not die.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two imperatives, רְדוּ and שִׁבְרוּ, 'go down and buy', are followed by וְנִחְיֶה, a cohortative: 'so that we may live'. No word for 'in order that' appears. The cohortative gives the aim of the two commands, and the negative וְלֹא נָמוּת, 'and not die', adds the other side.

quoted.title: Deuteronomy
quoted.english: that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren, and that he turn not aside from the commandment, to the right hand, or to the left; to the end that he may prolong his days in his kingdom, he and his children, in the midst of Israel.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Several aims are heaped on one command. לְבִלְתִּי with an infinitive twice gives the negative aims, 'so that his heart not be raised' and 'so that he not turn aside'. Then לְמַעַן with a yiqtol gives the positive aim, 'so that he may prolong his days'.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: For I will this time send all My plagues upon thy person, and upon thy servants, and upon thy people; that thou mayest know that there is none like Me in all the earth.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A condition, 'if you know'
A fear, 'lest you know'
An aim of the plagues: 'so that you may know that there is none like me'
A question
practice.explain: בַּעֲבוּר with a yiqtol, תֵּדַע, states the end for which God sends the plagues. The noun clause that follows with כִּי gives the content of what Pharaoh is to know.

practice.prompt: What does פֶּן־ (word 14) introduce in this speech?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: And they said: 'The God of the Hebrews hath met with us. Let us go, we pray thee, three days' journey into the wilderness, and sacrifice unto the LORD our God; lest He fall upon us with pestilence, or with the sword.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A wish, 'may he fall on us'
A thing feared: 'lest he fall on us', which is the reason for going to sacrifice
A condition, 'if he fall on us'
A result that has already happened
practice.explain: The speakers ask leave to go and sacrifice; פֶּן names the danger they hope to avoid by doing so. It is the language of fear: what they dread may or may not happen.

practice.prompt: What does the cohortative וְאֹכֵלָה (word 7) do after the imperatives?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: and make me savoury food, such as I love, and bring it to me, that I may eat; that my soul may bless thee before I die.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It gives the aim of the commands, 'that I may eat', before the further aim with בַּעֲבוּר
It is a second, unrelated command
It is a result that has already happened
It is a question
practice.explain: Isaac tells Esau to make food and bring it, and the cohortative says what that is for: so that he may eat. Then בַּעֲבוּר adds the further aim, that his soul may bless.

practice.prompt: How are the two clauses introduced by לְמַעַן (words 9 and 12) related to the command 'honour your father'?

quoted.title: Deuteronomy
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Each states a further aim of the command, joined by וּ
The second cancels the first
The first is a condition and the second a question
They are wishes for someone else
practice.explain: The command is followed by two clauses with לְמַעַן, each with a yiqtol. The second begins וּלְמַעַן and adds another end, 'that it may go well for you'. Stacked aims of this kind are frequent in Deuteronomy.

quoted.title: Deuteronomy
quoted.english: And now, O Israel, hearken unto the statutes and unto the ordinances, which I teach you, to do them; that ye may live, and go in and possess the land which the LORD, the God of your fathers, giveth you.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A past event
The aim of the teaching: 'which I teach you to do'
A condition
The reason for the teaching
practice.explain: The infinitive construct with לְ states what the teaching is for: that you may do them. The following clause with לְמַעַן gives a further aim, 'so that you may live'.

check.prompt: Why, according to this verse, did God not lead the people by the Philistine road?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: And it came to pass, when Pharaoh had let the people go, that God led them not by the way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near; for God said: 'Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war, and they return to Egypt.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: To avoid a feared result, introduced by פֶּן: lest the people repent when they see war
Because the road was far
Because the people had asked for another road
So that the people would live
check.explain: פֶּן־ names what God feared: that the people would change their mind when they met war. The fear explains the choice of road; the verse also says that the road was near, which is why it would have been tempting, not why God avoided it.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of men builded.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A command
The purpose of the LORD's coming down: 'to see the city'
A reason for the building
A condition
check.explain: The verb of motion וַיֵּרֶד is followed by an infinitive with לְ: the purpose of the descent. This is the commonest way to give a purpose.

check.prompt: What are לְהַצִּילוֹ and וּלְהַעֲלֹתוֹ (words 1 and 4) in relation to וָאֵרֵד?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: and I am come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians, and to bring them up out of that land unto a good land and a large, unto a land flowing with milk and honey; unto the place of the Canaanite, and the Hittite, and the Amorite, and the Perizzite, and the Hivite, and the Jebusite.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Two reasons given after the event
Two purposes of the descent, each an infinitive construct with a suffix naming the object
Two commands to Moses
A condition and its answer
check.explain: God came down to deliver them and to bring them up. Each infinitive carries the suffix 'him' (the people), and the second is joined to the first by וּ.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the LORD said unto him: 'Therefore whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold.' And the LORD set a sign for Cain, lest any finding him should smite him.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A wish
A command
A condition, 'unless'
The purpose of the sign, stated negatively: 'so that no one would strike him'
check.explain: לְבִלְתִּי with an infinitive gives a negative purpose. The LORD set a sign to protect Cain from being struck.

check.prompt: What are the weqatal verbs וְנוֹסַף, וְנִלְחַם and וְעָלָה (words 9, 14 and 16) doing?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: come, let us deal wisely with them, lest they multiply, and it come to pass, that, when there befalleth us any war, they also join themselves unto our enemies, and fight against us, and get them up out of the land.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: They narrate past events
They are commands to the Egyptians
They give what is feared in a chain after פֶּן: each event follows from the one before
They are wishes
check.explain: Pharaoh fears that the Israelites will multiply; the weqatals carry the fear on to what would follow, war, joining the enemies, and leaving the land. The whole series depends on פֶּן־.

check.prompt: How can לְמַעַן (word 14) be read in this verse of Amos?

quoted.title: Amos
quoted.english: That pant after the dust of the earth on the head of the poor, and turn aside the way of the humble; and a man and his father go unto the same maid, to profane My holy name;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: As purpose, 'in order to profane', or as result, 'so that the name is profaned'; both are grammatically possible
Only as a condition
Only as a purpose: the men aim to profane the name
It is a wish
check.explain: לְמַעַן with an infinitive is found with both senses. The purpose reading attributes the aim to the men; the result reading says only what their conduct brings about. The grammar does not decide.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And he said: 'Bring it near to me, and I will eat of my son's venison, that my soul may bless thee.' And he brought it near to him, and he did eat; and he brought him wine, and he drank.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A wish about someone else
A reason, 'because'
The aim of the eating: 'so that my soul may bless you'
A condition on the meal
check.explain: The imperative הַגִּשָׁה, 'bring near', and the cohortative וְאֹכְלָה, 'let me eat', are followed by the aim of it all: the blessing. לְמַעַן with a yiqtol states it.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: And the LORD said unto Moses: 'Lo, I come unto thee in a thick cloud, that the people may hear when I speak with thee, and may also believe thee for ever.' And Moses told the words of the people unto the LORD.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The aim of God's coming in the cloud: 'so that the people may hear'
A fear, 'lest the people hear'
A condition, 'if the people hear'
A past event
check.explain: God says that he will come in a thick cloud, and בַּעֲבוּר with a yiqtol gives the end. The next clause adds a second aim, with גַּם: the people will believe Moses too.

check.prompt: What does the clause with פֶּן־ (words 15 to 18) say about the commands before it?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And when the morning arose, then the angels hastened Lot, saying: 'Arise, take thy wife, and thy two daughters that are here; lest thou be swept away in the iniquity of the city.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It is another command
It gives the result that has already happened
It names the danger the commands (rise, take your wife and daughters) are meant to avoid
It gives a condition on which the commands depend
check.explain: The angels urge Lot to leave, and פֶּן־ states the danger if he does not: being swept away with the city. The yiqtol תִּסָּפֶה is a niphal, 'you be swept away'.

check.prompt: What does the pair of לְבִלְתִּי תֶחֱטָאוּ (words 17 and 18) with בַּעֲבוּר say?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The aim of the fear of God in them: 'so that you do not sin'
A condition: 'if you do not sin'
A wish that the people sin
A past event
check.explain: Moses says that the reverence for God will be upon their faces, and he states the end of it with the negative purpose לְבִלְתִּי and a yiqtol, 'so that you not sin'. The verb after לְבִלְתִּי may be a yiqtol as well as an infinitive.

reading.why: The tower story is full of the means this lesson names: cohortatives after הָבָה, a fear introduced by פֶּן, and a descent to see (לִרְאֹת). Reading it, you can mark each clause as purpose, fear or plain narrative.
